idiom_name: GCC/Clang variable cleanup attribute (`__attribute__((cleanup(fn)))`) with GLib g_auto/g_autoptr macros
implementation_notes: ISO C has no destructors, so the guard is either the cleanup variable attribute - a function attached to a local variable that runs when that variable goes out of scope, in reverse order of definition, and during stack unwinding when the translation unit is compiled with -fexceptions - or a single-exit goto-cleanup chain where the attribute is unavailable. GLib wraps the attribute in g_auto()/g_autoptr()/g_autofree() plus G_DEFINE_AUTOPTR_CLEANUP_FUNC(), so the cleanup function is declared once per type and the guard becomes one declaration at the point of acquisition; the classic owner-object structure is replaced by that declaration plus the compiler-generated call. The attribute is a GNU extension (GCC and clang only, not MSVC) and the cleanup function must return normally, so for portable or non-GNU toolchains the goto form remains the correct realization.
pitfalls: The attribute is a GNU extension: MSVC and strict/portable ISO C builds reject it, and the cleanup function must return normally - longjmp, exit or a non-local escape from it is undefined behaviour.

The cleanup function receives a pointer to the variable, so it sees the variable's final value: using a copy of the resource handle, or jumping over its initialisation, hands the function an indeterminate value.

Cleanup functions cannot report errors (no return value reaches the caller) and they run after the last statement of the scope, so per-resource error handling must happen before, not inside, the guard.

variants.name: Portable single-exit goto-cleanup chain
variants.idiom_name: single-exit `goto cleanup` chain with per-resource guards
variants.implementation_notes: Portable C89 realization: allocate each resource, remember it in a variable initialised to the 'none' value, and route every failure through a single exit label whose blocks release the resources in reverse order behind NULL/-1 checks; the label chain is the guard, and commit semantics are an explicit success flag rather than a dismissed object. Use this form when the cleanup attribute is unavailable (MSVC, embedded toolchains, strict ISO C) or when the release order must be visible in one place; it is weaker than a real guard because every early exit has to be rewritten as a jump, and any stray `return` bypasses the whole chain.
pitfalls: A single early `return` outside the chain bypasses every release; the discipline is only as strong as the rule that nobody returns early.
The label blocks release in one fixed order, so resources whose release must be conditional on success (commit versus rollback) need an explicit flag instead of a guard object.
